title: 25 famous psychology claims, retested on 58,653 people. 8 held up.
description:
25 claims people repeat as fact. We looked up the study each one came from, then looked up what happened when somebody ran it again.

58,653 people took part in the replications.
12 of the claims are gone - the retest could not tell them apart from nothing.
4 came back smaller but still measurable.
1 went the other way.
8 held up, 2 of them larger than the original.

Every episode, with the replication effect size and sample:
  bystander_effect         -0.35    7,700 people   held up
  ep003                    -0.23    1,550 people   held up
  ep007                    -0.87      776 people   held up
  ep011                    +0.65      743 people   held up
  ep015                    +0.34      740 people   held up
  ep017                    +0.36      321 people   held up
  ep018                    -0.85      240 people   held up
  sleep_memory             +0.29    2,004 people   held up
  ego_depletion            +0.04    2,141 people   gone
  ep000                    +0.01    6,608 people   gone
  ep001                    -0.07    1,283 people   gone
  ep002                    +0.08    1,086 people   gone
  ep004                    +0.13      997 people   gone
  ep005                    +0.22      823 people   smaller, still there
  ep006                    +0.40      723 people   smaller, still there
  ep008                    +0.18      564 people   smaller, still there
  ep009                    +0.14      556 people   gone
  ep010                    +0.06      488 people   gone
  ep012                    +0.03      404 people   gone

  ep014                    +0.08      316 people   gone

title: Learning styles: the one thing the idea needs came back at p = 0.29.
description:
Do you learn better when you are taught in your own style?

The claim as stated: Learning Styles: Concepts and Evidence (2009), doi:10.1111/j.1539-6053.2009.01038.x
The replication: Providing Instruction Based on Students' Learning Style Preferences Does Not Improve Learning (2020), n = 125, doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2020.00164

What the replication found:
  teaching to their style    F(1, 38) = 1.16   p = 0.290   not significant
  listening beat reading, for everyone F(1, 110) = 4.92, eta2 = 0.04   p = 0.030   significant
  visual types scored higher at both F(1, 32) = 12.92, eta2 = 0.29   p = 0.001   significant

Quoted from the replication:
  "There was not a significant main effect of instruction (F(1, 32) = 1.15, p = 0.29), nor an instruction by learning styles interaction (F(1, 38) = 1.16; p = 0.29)."
  "A significant main effect for instruction was found (F(1, 110) = 4.92; p = 0.03) with students performing better when listening (M = 36.0, SE = 0.9) than reading (M = 34.4, SE = 0.8). This corresponds to an effect size of eta 2 = 0.04, which is considered small."
  "There was a significant main effect of learning styles (auditory vs. visual; F (1, 32) = 12.92; p = 0.001) with an effect size of eta 2 = 0.29 ... These results indicate that visual learners were significantly better at both listening and reading comprehension, as compared to auditory learners."

The authors' own summary:
"Results failed to find a significant relationship between auditory or visual learning style preference and comprehension. Fifth graders with a visual learning style scored higher than those with an auditory learning style on listening and reading comprehension measures. As such, and counter to current educational beliefs and practices, teachers may actually be doing a disservice to students by using resources to determine their learning style and then tailoring the curriculum to match that learning style. [abstract]"

title: The backfire effect: the author says you read it wrong.
description:
Does correcting someone make them believe the wrong thing more?

The author says you read it wrong.

The original: When Corrections Fail: The Persistence of Political Misperceptions (2010)
  doi:10.1007/s11109-010-9112-2
  327 participants
The retest: The Elusive Backfire Effect: Mass Attitudes' Steadfast Factual Adherence (2019)
  doi:10.1007/s11109-018-9443-y
  10,100 participants
The original author, later: Why the backfire effect does not explain the durability of political misperceptions (2021)
  doi:10.1073/pnas.1912440117

What happened to the number:
  2010  conservatives in the control group   32%
  2010  a different group, given the correction   64%
  2019  issues retested for backfire   52
  2019  issues that actually backfired   0
  2021  the original author writes it up again

The original study:
"The experiments we present in this paper were all conducted in an online survey environment with undergraduates at a Catholic university in the Midwest."

The retest:
"We find that backfire is stubbornly difficult to induce, and is thus unlikely to be a characteristic of the public's relationship to factual information. Overwhelmingly, when presented with factual information that corrects politicians - even when the politician is an ally - the average subject accedes to the correction and distances himself from the inaccurate claim."

The original author, later:
"However, the scientific literature - including subsequent research that Reifler and I have conducted - does not support the interpretation that backfire effects explain the prevalence and durability of misperceptions."


What we could not verify first-hand:
  - Nothing missing for this episode.


How this channel works
The papers are read directly, and the sentence a number came from is quoted above wherever it is shown. Citation counts and some sample sizes are rounded down and always said as "more than", so the figure on screen is never larger than the real one. Where the original document could not be obtained, the number is left out rather than carried over from somebody's summary of it.

Not every episode is a debunking. Some of these findings held up, some turned out to be a problem with the original analysis rather than the result, and at least one is still an open argument.

title: Terror management theory: the original authors helped, and it still failed.
description:
Does thinking about your own death harden your beliefs?

The original authors helped, and it still failed.

The original: Role of consciousness and accessibility of death-related thoughts in mortality salience effects (1994)
  doi:10.1037/0022-3514.67.4.627
  59 participants
The retest: Many Labs 4: Failure to Replicate Mortality Salience Effect With and Without Original Author Involvement (2022)
  doi:10.1525/collabra.35271
  1,550 participants

What happened to the number:
  1994  the original study, 59 students   d = 1.34
  2022  ten labs, writing their own protocol
  2022  seven labs, advised by the original authors   g = 0.08
  2022  all of them together   g = 0.07

The original study:
"In the original study, a total of 59 introductory psychology students in the United States were randomly assigned between five conditions."

The retest:
"With 17 labs contributing usable data from 1,550 participants, we observed little evidence that priming mortality salience increased worldview defense compared to a control condition. We intended to use this paradigm to evaluate whether experts advising on the research protocol would increase effect sizes and overall replication success compared to independent In House replication attempts. However, neither the Author Advised nor In House protocols successfully replicated the original finding."


What we could not verify first-hand:
  - The In House labs' pooled effect size: the paper never reports one separately, only per-site values and the moderator coefficient.
